title: Dijkstra's algorithm
summary: Dijkstra grows a settled set by always taking the unsettled vertex of smallest distance. Every edge weight must be nonnegative. A binary heap runs in $O((|V|+|E|)\log|V|)$; the naive scan is $O(|V|^2)$.
intuition:
Dijkstra computes shortest-path weights from a source on a directed graph whose every edge weight is nonnegative. It keeps a distance label for each vertex, initially $0$ at the source and $\infty$ elsewhere. A vertex is settled when it is chosen as the unsettled vertex of smallest label. On settling $u$, every outgoing edge $u\to v$ of weight $w$ is relaxed: if $\mathrm{dist}(u)+w$ is smaller than $\mathrm{dist}(v)$, the label of $v$ is lowered. The invariant is that a settled label is final. It will not be improved by any later path.

Nonnegativity is the reason the invariant holds. When $b$ is settled, every unsettled vertex $a$ has $\mathrm{dist}(a)\ge \mathrm{dist}(b)$. An edge $a\to b$ of weight $w\ge 0$ then satisfies $\mathrm{dist}(a)+w\ge \mathrm{dist}(b)$, so it cannot undercut the settled label. A negative weight deletes that step. Take edges $s\to a$ of weight $4$, $s\to b$ of weight $3$, and $a\to b$ of weight $-2$. After $s$ is settled the labels are $\mathrm{dist}(a)=4$ and $\mathrm{dist}(b)=3$, so $b$ is settled next and frozen at $3$. The path $s\to a\to b$ weighs $4+(-2)=2$, which is smaller. The settled distance was not final. Zero weights are allowed; negative weights are not. When a weight may be negative, the algorithm that applies is Bellman-Ford, which is outside this basic syllabus.

The naive implementation finds the next minimum by scanning every unsettled label, $\Theta(|V|)$ work per settlement, for $O(|V|^2)$ overall. A binary heap makes each extraction and each relaxation $O(\log |V|)$, and there are $|V|$ extractions and at most $|E|$ successful relaxations, for $O((|V|+|E|)\log |V|)$. If every weight is $1$, the cheapest path is the path with the fewest edges, the layers are exactly the BFS layers, and the algorithm to run is BFS. That is the unweighted special case of the shortest-path problem. It is not a reason to replace the queue with Dijkstra's heap, and BFS remains a different algorithm.

definitions.body: For an edge $u\to v$ of weight $w$, replace $\mathrm{dist}(v)$ by $\mathrm{dist}(u)+w$ when that sum is smaller. Relaxation is the only way a label decreases.
A vertex removed from the unsettled set because its label is the smallest among unsettled vertices. Under nonnegative weights, that label equals the shortest-path weight and is never updated again.
A weight $w\ge 0$. Zero is nonnegative and is allowed. A single negative edge is enough to make a settled label improvable.
When every weight equals $1$, a shortest path is a path of fewest edges. BFS computes those distances with a queue. BFS is that special case of the problem, and it is not Dijkstra's heap algorithm.

formulas.name: Binary heap
formulas.note: Each of the $|V|$ extractions and each of the $|E|$ heap updates costs $O(\log |V|)$.

formulas.name: Naive scan
formulas.note: Finding the next unsettled minimum by a linear scan, repeated $|V|$ times. Fine for a dense graph, where $|E|$ is about $|V|^2$.

formulas.name: The inequality a negative weight breaks
formulas.note: At the moment $b$ is settled, $a$ is any still-unsettled vertex. A negative $w$ can reverse the last comparison.

properties: Every edge weight must be nonnegative. The settled distance is then the shortest-path weight.
A negative edge can leave a settled label strictly larger than the true distance, as when $4+(-2)=2$ undercuts a frozen label of $3$.
A binary heap gives $O((|V|+|E|)\log |V|)$. Scanning for the minimum gives $O(|V|^2)$.
Unweighted shortest paths are BFS. Equal weights of $1$ are the special case in which a queue replaces the priority queue.
The order of settlement is nondecreasing in distance. A later vertex never has a smaller shortest-path weight than an earlier one, while weights stay nonnegative.

examples.title: Four vertices, all weights positive
examples.prompt: Directed edges: $0\to 1$ weight $1$, $0\to 2$ weight $4$, $1\to 2$ weight $2$, $1\to 3$ weight $6$, $2\to 3$ weight $3$. Run Dijkstra from $0$.
steps: Settle $0$ with label $0$. Relaxation writes $\mathrm{dist}(1)=0+1=1$ and $\mathrm{dist}(2)=0+4=4$. Vertex $3$ is still $\infty$.
The smallest unsettled label is $1$, at vertex $1$. The edge $1\to 2$ replaces $4$ with $1+2=3$. The edge $1\to 3$ writes $1+6=7$.
The smallest unsettled label is now $3$, at vertex $2$, which beats $7$. The edge $2\to 3$ replaces $7$ with $3+3=6$. Vertex $3$ is settled last.
examples.answer: Settlement order is $0, 1, 2, 3$. The distances are $0, 1, 3, 6$, and their sum is $10$. The path to vertex $3$ is $0\to 1\to 2\to 3$, of weight $1+2+3=6$, against $7$ for $0\to 1\to 3$.

examples.title: Why the label 3 was not final
examples.prompt: Edges $s\to a$ weight $4$, $s\to b$ weight $3$, and $a\to b$ weight $-2$. Dijkstra settles a vertex once and then refuses to update it. What does it report for $b$, and what is the true weight?
steps: Vertex $b$ has the smaller unsettled label, so it is settled and frozen at $3$. Vertex $a$ is settled afterwards. The edge $a\to b$ is not allowed to change a settled label.
The ignored path weighs $4+(-2)=2$. If the same edge had weight $w\ge 0$, then $\mathrm{dist}(a)+w\ge 4\ge 3$, and the frozen label would have been safe. The hypothesis that failed is $w\ge 0$.
examples.answer: The frozen algorithm reports $3$. The true shortest-path weight is $2$. A settled distance is final only while every weight is nonnegative.

traps: Running Dijkstra on a graph that has a negative edge and trusting the first time a vertex is settled. The trace above freezes $b$ at $3$ when the cheapest path weighs $2$.
Replacing each negative weight by its absolute value and running Dijkstra. That is a different set of numbers, not a repair of the invariant.
Calling the binary-heap bound $O(|V|^2)$, or the naive scan $O((|V|+|E|)\log |V|)$. The heap is the first bound and the scan is the second.
Using Dijkstra for an unweighted graph and calling that BFS. Unweighted shortest paths are BFS. The heap algorithm is the nonnegative weighted algorithm.

questions.stem: Dijkstra is run from vertex $0$ on the directed edges $0\to 1$ weight $1$, $0\to 2$ weight $4$, $1\to 2$ weight $2$, $1\to 3$ weight $6$, and $2\to 3$ weight $3$. The shortest-path weight of vertex $3$ is
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**, $6$.

The path $0\to 1\to 2\to 3$ weighs $1+2+3=6$. The path $0\to 1\to 3$ weighs $7$, and $0\to 2\to 3$ weighs $4+3=7$. The minimum is $6$. Option B is either of those longer paths. Option D adds an edge that the winning path does not reuse.

questions.stem: The proof that a settled Dijkstra label is final assumes that
questions.solution:
The answer is **A**.

The comparison $\mathrm{dist}(a)+w\ge \mathrm{dist}(b)$ uses $w\ge 0$ together with the fact that an unsettled vertex cannot have a smaller label than the vertex being settled. Zero satisfies $w\ge 0$, so option B is stricter than the hypothesis. Option C is the unweighted special case, which BFS already solves. A tree is not required.
options: every edge weight is at least $1$, so a zero weight is forbidden

questions.stem: Which of the following are true?
questions.solution:
The correct options are **A, B, and C**.

A binary heap charges $O(\log |V|)$ for each extraction and each relaxation, which totals $O((|V|+|E|)\log |V|)$. Scanning all unsettled labels to find the next vertex is $O(|V|^2)$. The negative edge of weight $-2$ makes $4+(-2)=2$, undercutting a label frozen at $3$, so a settled distance need not be final once a weight is negative. Option D reverses the repair: absolute values are a different instance, and Dijkstra on that instance does not answer the original one.
options: With a binary heap the running time is $O((|V|+|E|)\log |V|)$.
The implementation that scans for the next minimum runs in $O(|V|^2)$.
A negative edge can leave a settled distance strictly worse than the true shortest-path weight.
A negative weight is handled by Dijkstra after every weight is replaced by its absolute value.

questions.stem: On the four-vertex nonnegative trace, which of the following are true?
questions.solution:
The correct options are **A, B, and C**.

The labels that get chosen are $0$, then $1$, then $3$ at vertex $2$, then $6$ at vertex $3$, so the order is $0, 1, 2, 3$. Settling vertex $1$ replaces the label $4$ on vertex $2$ by $1+2=3$. The direct route from $1$ to $3$ weighs $6$, and $1+6=7$, which loses to $6$. Option D is false: after vertex $0$ is settled, vertex $3$ still has no finite label.
options: The vertices are settled in the order $0, 1, 2, 3$.
The label of vertex $2$ is updated from $4$ to $3$ when vertex $1$ is settled.
The walk $0\to 1\to 3$ has weight $7$, which is worse than the weight of $0\to 1\to 2\to 3$.
The label of vertex $3$ is final as soon as vertex $0$ is settled.

questions.stem: On that same four-vertex run from vertex $0$, what is the sum of the four shortest-path weights?
questions.solution:
The answer is **10**.

The weights are $0$, $1$, $3$, and $6$. Their sum is $0+1+3+6=10$. The $0$ is the source and is part of the sum.
